analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 500% excise tax on corporate money spent in federal campaigns.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsor bill to tax corporate campaign spending at 500% died in the Ways and Means Committee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed a 500% tax on every dollar a corporation contributes to political committees or spends on ads that promote or attack a federal candidate, and denied corporations any tax deduction for paying it. A dollar of corporate campaign spending would have cost six dollars, effectively pricing most corporations out of federal electioneering. It was introduced by one House member, referred to the tax-writing committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would see less corporate money in federal elections. Candidates and groups that rely on small donors would face less competition from corporate-funded advertising, and federal officeholders would face less pressure from corporate spenders.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax equal to 500% of a corporation's total contributions to political committees plus its spending on electioneering communications — broadcast ads that mention a federal candidate — making each dollar of corporate campaign spending cost six dollars. [S3]
Denies corporations an income tax deduction for the tax, so the cost could not be passed to taxpayers as a write-off. [S2]

Directs that any court determination that campaign finance law does not apply to corporations be disregarded — language aimed at rulings, like the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision issued days after introduction, that opened corporate election spending. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that spend money on federal elections and the broadcast and media companies that sell the political advertising time. Shareholders of politically active corporations would also bear the cost through reduced returns.

drawbacks.text: A 500% tax on spending to communicate about candidates would likely face a serious First Amendment challenge after the Supreme Court's Citizens United ruling protected corporate independent spending — the bill's own text anticipates this by directing courts' determinations to be disregarded, a provision that itself may be beyond what a statute can do. [S3]

The bill covers corporations but not other big spenders such as unions, and applies to contributions and electioneering ads rather than all political spending, so a court or Congress could be pressed to broaden or narrow it in ways that raise fairness questions. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — sharply less corporate money in federal elections — is real and large for anyone who wants campaigns decided by voters rather than corporate treasuries. The constitutional risk is genuine: the Supreme Court had just held that corporate independent spending is protected speech, and a punitive 500% tax aimed squarely at that spending would be tested immediately. As designed, the bill is a blunt instrument, and it never went through a committee process that could have addressed those questions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the bill on January 13, 2010, eight days before the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision. [S1]
The same day it was introduced, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means. [S5]
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote. [S5]
No other member of the House cosponsored it. [S4]
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and the political advertising industry, which kept the ability to spend unlimited amounts on federal elections without a 500% tax. Nothing about the status quo changed for them, and no committee ever weighed the proposal on its merits.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it as a response to corporate election spending; no colleague joined him.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for consideration, letting it die without a vote.

against.name: House members of both parties
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, including none of the 252 other House Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill attracted support only from its Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: Corporations would have paid six dollars for every dollar spent on federal campaign contributions and candidate ads. Their interest in cheap political influence runs against voters' interest in elections less dominated by corporate money.

industries.industry: Broadcast and media companies selling political ads
industries.note: Electioneering communications are the expensive broadcast ads that mention federal candidates; a 500% tax on them would sharply shrink a lucrative ad market.
